def-cox-proportional-hazards-model-and-p:
## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Assume the conditional right-censoring observation scheme of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. Conditional independence of event and censoring given the covariate history is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification is a parametric statistical model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]]. It consists of a parameter $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$ \Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du. $$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$ Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}. $$
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$ S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}. $$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$ \frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}. $$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$ L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}. $$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$ \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}. $$
If instead a continuous-time ordering is coarsened into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Summing over the unobserved within-interval failure order gives the ordered-risk-set conditional contribution
$$ \sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}. $$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
These are exact likelihoods for their stated tie conventions; they are not interchangeable without a model relating those conventions. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$ L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}} $$
and
$$ L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}. $$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.
lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence:
## Statement

Let $O_i=(T_i,C_i,Z_i(\cdot))$, $i\ge1$, be IID subject records with law $P$, with jointly measurable predictable covariates, $p<\infty$, and $\|Z_i(t)\|_2\le K$ for all $i,t$ outside one null event. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^p$ be compact and contain $\beta_0$. With $Y_i(t)=1\{U_i\ge t\}$, define, for $r=0,1,2$,
$$ S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)},\qquad s^{(r)}(t,\beta)=E_P[Y_i(t)Z_i(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ_i(t)}], $$
where $Z^{\otimes0}=1$, $Z^{\otimes1}=Z$, and $Z^{\otimes2}=ZZ^T$. Suppose $c_0:=\inf_{t\le\tau}s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)>0$. For every finite deterministic measure $\nu(dt)=w(t)\,dt$ with nonnegative integrable density $w$, put
$$ D_n(t)=\max_{r=0,1,2}\sup_{\beta\in B}\|S_n^{(r)}(t,\beta)-s^{(r)}(t,\beta)\|_{\max}. $$
Then for each fixed $t$, $E[D_n(t)^2]\to0$, and
$$ E\int_0^\tau D_n(t)^2\,\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0. $$
There are measurable events $E_n$ with $P(E_n)\to1$ and a constant $c>0$ such that on $E_n$,
$$ S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)\ge c\qquad\text{for every }t\le\tau,\  eta\in B. $$
Define $\bar Z_n=S_n^{(1)}/S_n^{(0)}$ and $V_n=S_n^{(2)}/S_n^{(0)}-\bar Z_n\bar Z_n^T$, setting each to zero at a zero denominator, and define $\bar z=s^{(1)}/s^{(0)}$, $V=s^{(2)}/s^{(0)}-\bar z\bar z^T$. Their fixed-time and integrated parameter-uniform errors satisfy
$$ E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|\bar Z_n(t,\beta)-\bar z(t,\beta)\|_2^2\to0,\qquad E\sup_{\beta\in B}\|V_n(t,\beta)-V(t,\beta)\|_{\max}^2\to0, $$
$$ E\int_0^\tau\sup_{\beta\in B}\!\left\{\|\bar Z_n-\bar z\|_2^2+\|V_n-V\|_{\max}^2\right\}\nu(dt)\longrightarrow0. $$
These conclusions require no regularity of the time-indexed covariate class beyond bounded predictability. In particular take $\nu(dt)=\lambda_0(t)\,dt$.

The stronger uniform-in-time conclusion remains valid under the following additional, sufficient condition: every scalar coordinate class $\mathcal F_{r,k}=\{O\mapsto[Y(t)Z(t)^{\otimes r}e^{\beta^TZ(t)}]_k:t\le\tau,\beta\in B\}$ is pointwise measurable and has finite $L^1(P)$ bracketing number at every positive width. Under that condition, $\sup_tD_n(t)\to_P0$, and both ratio errors converge uniformly on $[0,\tau]\times B$ in probability. This optional condition is not imposed by the Cox inference consumers.
lem-bounded-predictable-counting-integra:
## Statement

Under [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], for every nonnegative predictable $G$,
$$ E\int_{(0,T]}G_t\,dN_t=E\int_0^T G_t\,dA_t. $$
For every bounded real predictable $H$, the L²-completed stochastic integral equals the pathwise finite-variation expression almost surely:
$$ \int_0^T H_t\,dM_t=\sum_{0<t\le T}H_t\Delta N_t-\int_0^T H_t\,dA_t,\qquad M=N-A. $$
The identity holds at every fixed terminal time and coordinatewise for vector or matrix integrands. No left continuity of $H$ is assumed.
lem-cox-partial-likelihood-hessian-conve:
## Statement

Use the IID bounded-covariate setup and the risk-support and compact-set hypotheses of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]]. For each subject let $N_i(t)=1\{U_i\le t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $A_i(t)=\int_0^tY_i(u)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(u)}\lambda_0(u)\,du$. Assume the continuous counting-process contract of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]] for each $M_i=N_i-A_i$ on one common filtration, and assume no two subjects fail at the same time. Write $N_\cdot=\sum_iN_i$, $A_\cdot=\sum_iA_i$, and $\mathcal M=N_\cdot-A_\cdot$. For $\beta\in B$, let
$$ V_n(t,\beta)=\frac{S_n^{(2)}(t,\beta)}{S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)} -\bar Z_n(t,\beta)\bar Z_n(t,\beta)^T,\qquad V(t,\beta)=\frac{s^{(2)}(t,\beta)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta)} -\bar z(t,\beta)\bar z(t,\beta)^T, $$
using zero values when a finite-sample denominator is zero. Let $U_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta\log L_p(\beta)$ and $H_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta U_n(\beta)^T$. Define
$$ J(\beta)=\int_0^\tau V(t,\beta)s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)\lambda_0(t)\,dt. $$
Then the partial log-likelihood Hessian satisfies
$$ \sup_{\beta\in B}\left\|n^{-1}H_n(\beta)+J(\beta)\right\|_{\max}\longrightarrow_P0. $$
The map $J:B\to\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ is continuous.
In particular, $J(\beta_0)=I$, where
$$ I=\int_0^\tau\left\{s^{(2)}(t,\beta_0)- \frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)^T}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}\right\}\lambda_0(t)\,dt. $$
lem-cox-score-martingale-replacement:
## Statement

Use the IID bounded-covariate model, risk-support hypotheses of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]], the no-tie event process, and the per-subject counting-process contracts of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Let
$$ \bar z(t)=\frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)},\qquad I=\int_0^\tau\left\{s^{(2)}(t,\beta_0)- \frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)^T}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}\right\}\lambda_0(t)\,dt,\qquad \xi_i=\int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t), $$
where each vector integral is defined coordinatewise in L². If $U_n(\beta)=\partial_\beta\log L_p(\beta)$ is the partial-likelihood score, then
$$ n^{-1/2}U_n(\beta_0)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i+o_P(1). $$
The $\xi_i$ are IID, centered, square-integrable vectors with covariance matrix $I$. In particular, $n^{-1/2}\sum_i\xi_i=O_P(1)$. The replacement of the random risk-set mean by $\bar z$ is part of the conclusion.
thm-cox-score-limit-and-estimator-linear:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p<\infty$, $\tau>0$, and $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$. Let subjects $O_i=(T_i,C_i,Z_i(\cdot))$ be IID and independent. Assume the Cox model of [[def-cox-proportional-hazards-model-and-partial-likelihood]] with bounded predictable covariates $\|Z_i(t)\|_2\le K$, baseline $\lambda_0\in L^1[0,\tau]$, and no tied failures. Assume the positive population risk denominators of [[lem-cox-uniform-risk-set-convergence]] on a compact neighborhood $B$ of $\beta_0$. In one common filtration, assume the observed event counts $N_i(t)=1\{U_i\le t,\delta_i=1\}$ have compensators
$$ A_i(t)=\int_0^tY_i(u)e^{\beta_0^TZ_i(u)}\lambda_0(u)\,du $$
and that $M_i=N_i-A_i$ satisfies the square-integrable counting-process contract of [[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. This martingale contract is an explicit model assumption. No bracketing or time-class regularity is required: the risk-set lemma supplies the integrated parameter-uniform laws for these bounded predictable paths.

Let $I$ be the matrix in [[lem-cox-partial-likelihood-hessian-convergence]] and assume $I$ is positive definite. Let $\hat\beta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^p$-valued estimator such that, with probability tending to one, it solves the partial-likelihood score equation $U_n(\hat\beta_n)=0$, and suppose $\hat\beta_n\to_P\beta_0$. Then
$$ \sqrt n(\hat\beta_n-\beta_0) =I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \int_0^\tau\{Z_i(t)-\bar z(t)\}\,dM_i(t)+o_P(1), \qquad \bar z(t)=\frac{s^{(1)}(t,\beta_0)}{s^{(0)}(t,\beta_0)}. $$
The proof establishes the partial-likelihood score representation locally; it does not treat the score summands with the random risk-set mean as IID.
cor-cox-partial-likelihood-asymptotic-no:
## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of [[thm-cox-score-limit-and-estimator-linearization]] and AC. Then
$$
\sqrt n(\hat\beta_n-\beta_0)\ \Rightarrow\ N_p(0,I^{-1}).
$$
This terminal normal limit follows from the separately proved influence expansion; it is not used to prove that expansion.
